newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: India, Bangladesh eye trade after water accord.
newsitem.headline: India, Bangladesh eye trade after water accord.

text.p: A landmark water-sharing treaty between India and Bangladesh has opened the floodgates for long-term economic cooperation, analysts said on Tuesday.

"The treaty gives a solid start to cooperation, maybe in the long term, as business understandings have been changing fast in south Asia and beyond," Atiur Rahman of the Bangladesh Institute of Development Studies told Reuters.
"Bangladesh may not have reaped any major dividend immediately, except for getting water from the river Ganges, but in the long run it can benefit immensely."

The two countries signed the 30-year treaty in New Delhi in December, removing what had been the biggest obstacle to cooperation. The treaty covers the distribution of water from the Ganges and the share each nation gets.
Some 40 million people, or one-third of the population of Bangladesh -- which is down-stream -- rely on the river for their livelihood. But the flow can change dramatically depending on the season.
Analysts said the Bangladesh accord would immediately benefit agriculture, navigation and the environment.
It could lead to similar accords on 50 other common rivers, open a controversial trade route for India and spark foreign investment, they said.
But most importantly, it has created a better atmosphere for economic cooperation, which Bangladesh ultimately hopes will close its US$1.03 billion trade deficit with India.
"It has created a ground for negotiations on all matters in our bilateral relations. It has a tremendous political impact and people will look for eventual economic gains," Rahman said.
"Both sides are doing themselves a favour," said B.G. Verghese of New Delhi's Centre for Policy Research.
But analysts said both countries had yet to work out any concrete plans and there were still differences over the parameters of the agreement.

Indian officials said Dhaka, which for more than a decade insisted on a Ganges water accord as a condition for discussion of other issues, was now in a position to offer New Delhi a transit route through Bangladesh.
It would link India's seven hilly northeastern states, which curl around the north and east of Bangladesh, with the Indian heartland.
"This could make available natural gas reserves from the northeast, and also help establish power transmission lines through Bangladesh to the northeast," Verghese said.
Indian Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral is due in Nepal on Thursday to give effect to a separate water-sharing agreement with the Himalayan kingdom.
Analysts said Bangladesh was not linking its water agreement with other issues.
"The water treaty has no direct relationship with economic and trade issues," said water expert and Dhaka University lecturer Ainun Nishat.

But he added: "After the treaty, the door has been opened to pursuing issues in the economic and trade sectors. Without the solution of water issues the government could not move to resolve the trade and economic problems.
"So far we either got too much water or too little which is not desireable for our economy. After the treaty we will be able to get water as per our requirements.
"Other (common) rivers will now come under the treaty gradually. Ecological degradation will stop."
